monoclonal_antibodies.abstract: Abstract Multi-agent-based simulations (MABS) of electric vehicle (EV) home charging ecosystems generate large, complex, and stochastic time-series datasets that capture interactions between households, grid infrastructure, and energy markets. These interactions can lead to unexpected system-level events, such as transformer overloads or consumer dissatisfaction, that are difficult to detect and explain through static post-processing. This paper presents a modular, Python-based dashboard framework—built using Dash by Plotly—that enables efficient, multi-level exploration and root-cause analysis of emergent behavior in MABS outputs. The system features three coordinated views (System Overview, System Analysis, and Consumer Analysis), each offering high-resolution visualizations such as time-series plots, spatial heatmaps, and agent-specific drill-down tools. A case study simulating full EV adoption with smart charging in a Danish residential network demonstrates how the dashboard supports rapid identification and contextual explanation of anomalies, including clustered transformer overloads and time-dependent charging failures. The framework facilitates actionable insight generation for researchers and distribution system operators, and its architecture is adaptable to other distributed energy resources and complex energy systems. Computer Science > Networking and Internet Architecture arXiv:2610.20222 (cs) [Submitted on 14 Oct 2026] Title: A Multiarmed Bandit Approach for LTE-U/Wi-Fi Coexistence in a Multicell Scenario Authors: Iago Diógenes do Rego , José M. de Castro Neto , Sildolfo F. G. Neto , Pedro M. de Santana , Vicente A. de Sousa Jr. , Dario Vieira , Augusto Venâncio Neto View a PDF of the paper titled A Multiarmed Bandit Approach for LTE-U/Wi-Fi Coexistence in a Multicell Scenario, by Iago Di\'ogenes do Rego and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Recent studies and literature reviews have shown promising results for 3GPP system solutions in unlicensed bands when coexisting with Wi-Fi, either by using the duty cycle (DC) approach or licensed-assisted access (LAA). However, it is widely known that general performance in these coexistence scenarios is dependent on traffic and how the duty cycle is adjusted. Most DC solutions configure their parameters statically, which can result in performance losses when the scenario experiences changes on the offered data. In our previous works, we demonstrated that reinforcement learning (RL) techniques can be used to adjust DC parameters. We showed that a Q-learning (QL) solution that adapts the LTE DC ratio to the transmitted data rate can maximize the Wi-Fi/LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U) aggregated throughput. In this paper, we extend our previous solution by implementing a simpler and more efficient algorithm based on multiarmed bandit (MAB) theory. We evaluate its performance and compare it with the previous one in different traffic scenarios. The results demonstrate that our new solution offers improved balance in throughput, providing similar results for LTE and Wi-Fi, while still showing a substantial system gain. Moreover, in one of the scenarios, our solution outperforms the previous approach by 6% in system throughput. In terms of user throughput, it achieves more than 100% gain for the users at the 10th percentile of performance, while the old solution only achieves a 10% gain. Computer Science > Information Retrieval arXiv:2610.24030 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Oct 2026] Title: When Does Evidence-Graph Structure Predict Answer Correctness? Label-Free Abstention for Structured Retrieval Authors: Anjan Goswami View a PDF of the paper titled When Does Evidence-Graph Structure Predict Answer Correctness? Label-Free Abstention for Structured Retrieval, by Anjan Goswami View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Retrieval systems return scored answers, but a high score does not show that an answer should be trusted. The proposed training-free abstention method applies the boundary cut to the selected evidence in an evidence graph. The signal is the weighted cut between selected and unselected candidates and requires no correctness labels or confidence-model training. On MemoryAgentBench (MAB) FactConsolidation multi-hop, with unresolved queries ranked last for every selector, it raises area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 for the best score baseline to 0.785 (+0.049, 95% CI [+0.008, +0.092]); under the native evaluation, where score baselines keep their unresolved values, the gap is +0.108. A zero-cut subset contains 71 of 400 queries at 100% observed precision. In this pipeline, the subset corresponds to structural closure; controlled analyses attribute much of the remaining separation to resolution status, with little benefit from continuous edge weights. Across external benchmarks, usefulness varies with graph construction, edge semantics, and relation; typed structure alone does not ensure useful confidence. A supervised gradient-boosted selector achieves 0.814 versus the boundary cut's 0.785 when the retrieval stack matches. These findings provide empirical guidance for using available evidence graphs for lightweight, auditable post-retrieval abstention without additional model inference. Comments: 34 pages, 5 figures, 37 tables. Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2610.26474 (cs) [Submitted on 19 Oct 2026] Title: AfriGuard: Safety and Robust Refusal For African Languages Authors: Israel Abebe Azime , Jesujoba O. Alabi , Iffat Maab , Alexander D. Cai , Tadesse Destaw Belay , Atnafu Lambebo Tonja , Jonas Kgomo , Folasade Alabi , Salomey Osei , Saminu Muhammad Aliyu , Nkechinyere Faith Aguobi , Bontu Fufa Balcha , Blessing Sibanda , Davis David , Mouhamadane Mboup , Daud Abolade , Neo Putini , Louis Powell , Kiant'e Brantley , Philipp Slusallek , Dietrich Klakow , Julia Kreutzer View a PDF of the paper titled AfriGuard: Safety and Robust Refusal For African Languages, by Israel Abebe Azime and 21 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) designed to interact with users are typically trained to respond appropriately to harmful or toxic content. However, ensuring appropriate responses becomes more challenging in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts, where safety risks may be expressed or interpreted differently. Building safe AI systems therefore requires detecting safety risks, understanding their nature, and responding appropriately, while accounting for linguistic and cultural variations that add complexity to each stage. In this work, we introduce AfriGuard, a culturally grounded multilingual dataset for studying harmful intent, safety-category understanding, and refusal behavior across 10 African languages and English. Our findings reveal that guardrail models underperform both open- and closed-source LLMs on safety-intent and safety-category classification, while models show limited understanding of appropriate safety behavior, scoring below 60% F1. We further find that models often fail to respond appropriately to unsafe prompts not because they explicitly refuse, but because they produce linguistically inadequate responses that result in incidental non-assistance rather than proper refusals. Finally, using AfriGuard, we develop efficient guardrail models that achieve performance competitive with models up to 30x larger, introduce refusal detectors that improve average performance by 43.9% over existing detectors, and demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning can substantially improve overall safety performance.
